Series::calc¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

Series::CalcAccessor Series::calc
const Series::CalcAccessor& Series::calc() const noexcept
Series::CalcAccessor Series::calc(const Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions& options) const

What It Does¶

calc is the entrypoint for calculus on a callable. The owning Series has a different role in the two directions:

  • for diff(), grad(), jac(), and hess(), it is the independent value at which the callable is differentiated;

  • for antidiff(), it is the upper endpoint of an anchored integral.

Accessing calc does not evaluate the callback, record a persistent graph, or copy the receiver. A terminal method selects the operation and invokes the callback with a temporary differentiable or quadrature-node Series.

Open the dedicated Series::CalcAccessor API Reference for the complete method family, tensor-shape conventions, and option table.

Why This Is Separate¶

Series already has two similarly named sequence operations, but neither takes a callable:

  • Series::diff() subtracts adjacent stored samples.

  • Series::antidiff integrates stored samples with trapezoids.

calc instead asks a function for values as needed. x.calc.diff(fn) differentiates the expression built by fn(x), while upper.calc.antidiff(fn, lower) evaluates fn at quadrature nodes between two endpoints. The separation prevents a sampled sequence from being mistaken for the function that generated it.

Calling Styles¶

The member and zero-argument call forms are equivalent:

auto dot = x.calc.diff(fn);
auto call = x.calc().diff(fn);

Passing CalcOptions creates a lightweight accessor with those defaults bound:

Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;

auto second = x.calc(options);
auto value = second.diff(fn);

The receiver and its numeric storage are not copied. The returned accessor keeps the receiver binding plus its own option record, so separate configured accessors may be used independently.

Examples¶

Example 1. Dot and call syntax select the same first derivative.

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.5);
auto fn = [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.sin(); };

std::cout << x.calc.diff(fn) << "\n";
std::cout << x.calc().diff(fn) << "\n";

Output¶

data=0.87758256
data=0.87758256

Example 2. Bound options organize several calls around one calculus policy.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.5);
auto configured = x.calc(options);

std::cout << configured.diff(
    [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.sin(); }) << "\n";
std::cout << "order=" << configured.options().order << "\n";

Output¶

data=-0.47942554
order=2

Example 3. The same entrypoint makes the receiver an integration endpoint.

auto upper = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
auto area = upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.square(); }, 0.0);

std::cout << area << "\n";

Output¶

data=[0.041666667, 0.33333333, 2.6666667]

Each endpoint is independent: the result is [integral_0^0.5 t^2 dt, integral_0^1 t^2 dt, integral_0^2 t^2 dt] and keeps the receiver’s shape.

Lifetime And Mutation¶

The accessor is cheap, but it remains bound to its receiver. Do not retain an accessor beyond the lifetime of the Series that created it. Terminal methods return new Series values and do not mutate the receiver.
